items.title: Add pacman package manager commands
items.body:
Version: `git-pkgs/managers` current `main` at [`241e284`](https://github.com/git-pkgs/managers/commit/241e28416122e0c1f79aa5c590fe4f154e0a58ce).

Trying to build an Arch package operation after registering the embedded definitions currently returns `unknown manager: pacman`:

```go
_, err := tr.BuildCommand("pacman", "add", managers.CommandInput{
	Args: map[string]string{"package": "core/bash", "version": "5.3.3-1"},
})
```

Add a `pacman` definition for Arch's system package manager. Include `definitions/pacman.yaml`, captured version and command help under `references/pacman`, translator tests, and Docker coverage as described in the [new manager contribution guide](https://github.com/git-pkgs/managers/blob/241e28416122e0c1f79aa5c590fe4f154e0a58ce/CONTRIBUTING.md#L3-L20).

Pacman has no project manifest or lockfile, so this definition should be selected explicitly through `DetectOptions.Manager`. A `PKGBUILD` belongs to the `makepkg` build flow and should not trigger this installed-package manager.

Use the native pacman operations:

- Map `add` to `pacman -S --needed --noconfirm PACKAGE` and `remove` to `pacman -R --noconfirm PACKAGE`. The [`pacman(8)` sync documentation](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/blob/a6f7467d8c7c4d7e9cc846884e74c0ab7215c48d/doc/pacman.8.asciidoc#L49-96) covers repository-qualified targets such as `testing/qt` and constraints such as `bash>=3.2`.
- Map `list` to `pacman -Q`, `outdated` to `pacman -Qu`, and `update` to `pacman -Syu --noconfirm`. The [query options](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/blob/a6f7467d8c7c4d7e9cc846884e74c0ab7215c48d/doc/pacman.8.asciidoc#L315-390) define installed and upgrade filtering.
- Keep repository refresh and system upgrade in the same `-Syu` transaction. The [sync options](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/blob/a6f7467d8c7c4d7e9cc846884e74c0ab7215c48d/doc/pacman.8.asciidoc#L430-483) describe `-u` and recommend using `-y` with it. `outdated` should query the current sync database without silently running `pacman -Sy` first.

The generic `install` operation has no package set to pass to `pacman -S`, so leave it unsupported unless the public API gains a safe way to provide the desired packages. Pacman's `-T` operation checks named dependency constraints but does not return a dependency graph. `-Ql` returns all files owned by a package rather than one package directory. Do not advertise `resolve` or `path` for those commands.

Repository URLs are configured in `pacman.conf`, while a command can select a configured repository with the `repository/package` target syntax. The checked-in [`pacman.conf` template](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/blob/a6f7467d8c7c4d7e9cc846884e74c0ab7215c48d/etc/pacman.conf.in#L1-125) provides an example configuration file for tests and documentation.

Reuse the per-command privilege metadata requested in [#30](https://github.com/git-pkgs/managers/issues/30). Generated commands should not prepend `sudo`; callers need to choose how system-changing operations are elevated. Use pacman's documented [`--noconfirm`](https://gitlab.archlinux.org/pacman/pacman/-/blob/a6f7467d8c7c4d7e9cc846884e74c0ab7215c48d/doc/pacman.8.asciidoc#L180-196) flag for non-interactive mutations.

Tests should cover repository-qualified names, exact and range versions, `--needed`, non-interactive add and remove commands, installed and outdated listings, the atomic `-Syu` update, and privilege metadata. Include cases proving that `outdated` does not refresh repositories and that unsupported `install`, `resolve`, and `path` capabilities are not declared.

items.title: Resolution failure depends on order of dependencies: exhausted attempts to resolve the dependencies graph
items.body:
### Is it reproducible with SwiftPM command-line tools: `swift build`, `swift test`, `swift package` etc?

- [x] Confirmed reproduction steps with SwiftPM CLI. The description text _must_ include reproduction steps with either of command-line SwiftPM commands, `swift build`, `swift test`, `swift package` etc.

### Description

I was investigating how SwiftPM handles certain edge cases related to traits (while trying to reproduce SwiftPM package graph loading logic in my own project), and discovered this edge case that SwiftPM doesn't appear to handle.

I have a root package that depends on both `SecondLibrary` and `ThirdLibrary`. Both of those packages depend on another library called `Library`. `SecondLibrary` doesn't enable any of `Library`'s traits, while `ThirdLibrary` enables `Library`'s `MyTrait` trait. If `MyTrait` is enabled, `Library` pulls in [swift-concurrency-extras](https://github.com/pointfreeco/swift-concurrency-extras) (which I was using a placeholder for presumably any remote package).

If `SecondLibrary` comes before `ThirdLibrary` in the root package's dependencies list then SwiftPM package resolution fails;

```console
$ swift run
error: exhausted attempts to resolve the dependencies graph, with the following dependencies unresolved:
* 'swift-concurrency-extras' from https://github.com/pointfreeco/swift-concurrency-extras
```

If `ThirdLibrary` comes before `SecondLibrary` then package resolution consistently succeeds (and checks out `swift-concurrency-extras`).

Importantly, a clean build is required after switching the ordering back to the one that causes failures, otherwise some cached information from the 'good' ordering makes package resolution succeed until the next clean build.

### Expected behavior

Package graph resolution succeeds regardless of dependency ordering, and `Library` ends up with the `MyTrait` trait enabled in both cases.

### Actual behavior

Package resolution fails when `SecondLibrary` comes before `ThirdLibrary` in the dependencies list of the root package.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create the test packages by either downloading my zip of test packages or constructing the packages manually using the package manifests included inline below.
2. Run `swift run` and observe that package resolution fails
3. Swap the order of `SecondLibrary` and `ThirdLibrary` in the root Package.swift file
4. Run `swift run` again and observe that package resolution succeeds

I've packaged up my group of test packages here: [TraitsRepro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31718804/TraitsRepro.zip)

Alternatively, you can create the packages yourself using the following package manifests as a reference;
<details>
<summary>Package.swift</summary>

```swift
// swift-tools-version: 6.3

import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "TraitsRepro",
    platforms: [.macOS(.v10_15)],
    dependencies: [
        .package(path: "SecondLibrary"),
        .package(path: "ThirdLibrary"),
    ],
    targets: [
        .executableTarget(
            name: "TraitsRepro",
            dependencies: ["SecondLibrary", "ThirdLibrary"]
        ),
    ]
)
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Library/Package.swift</summary>

```swift
// swift-tools-version: 6.3

import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Library",
    platforms: [.macOS(.v10_15)],
    products: [
        .library(
            name: "Library",
            targets: ["Library"]
        ),
    ],
    traits: [
        .trait(name: "MyTrait"),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(url: "https://github.com/pointfreeco/swift-concurrency-extras", from: "1.4.1"),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "Library",
            dependencies: [
                .product(name: "ConcurrencyExtras", package: "swift-concurrency-extras", condition: .when(traits: ["MyTrait"])),
            ]
```

```swift
    name: "SecondLibrary",
    platforms: [.macOS(.v10_15)],
    products: [
        .library(
            name: "SecondLibrary",
            targets: ["SecondLibrary"]
        ),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(path: "../Library"),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "SecondLibrary",

        ),
    ]
```

Real Studio-generated apps can report a complete Bun v2 status graph and still fail native planning after APM stages reviewed direct updates and asks Bun to rewrite the lockfile:

items.title: Support package maps
items.body:
### 🔍 Search Terms

package map, package maps, package-map.json, `--experimental-package-map`, static module resolution, phantom dependencies, undeclared dependencies, isolated dependencies, yarn pnp, pnpm, moduleResolution

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Node.js 26.4 added [**package maps**](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#package-maps) (experimental, enabled with `--experimental-package-map=<path>`). A package map is a static JSON file that tells the runtime, for each package, exactly which bare specifiers it can import and where they live on disk. When it's enabled, Node doesn't walk `node_modules` folders to resolve bare specifiers. It looks them up in the map.

Package managers already generate these files: Yarn and pnpm can both emit a package map as part of an install, and bundlers have started early experiments with it (for example Vite). It's becoming a shared, tool-agnostic description of "what this project's dependency graph looks like on disk."

I'd like TypeScript to read a package map and use it in module resolution, so that the type checker resolves bare specifiers the same way the runtime does. Concretely, I'm suggesting a new compiler option that points to the file:

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "packageMap": "./node_modules/.package-map.json"
  }
}
```

This option would **not** add a new `moduleResolution` mode. It would replace one step of the existing algorithms, the `node_modules` directory lookup that finds a package's root folder. Everything after that step (`exports`/`imports` conditions, `types`/`typesVersions`, extension substitution, `.d.ts` lookup) would stay exactly as it is today under `node16`, `nodenext`, or `bundler`. That's also how Node specifies it: the map gives you a package location, and the regular resolution algorithm takes it from there.

#### The file format

The map is a single static JSON file. Each entry under `packages` is keyed by an opaque **package ID**, and has:

- `url` (required): the package's location, resolved relative to the map file. Only `file:` URLs are supported.
- `dependencies` (optional): an object that maps each bare specifier the package may import to the package ID it resolves to.

```json
{
  "packages": {
    "app": {
      "url": "./packages/app",
      "dependencies": {
        "@myorg/utils": "utils",
        "react": "react@18.3.1",
        "@types/react": "@types/react@18.3.3"
      }
    },
    "utils": {
      "url": "./packages/utils"
    },
    "react@18.3.1": {
      "url": "./node_modules/.store/react@18.3.1/package"
    },
    "@types/react@18.3.3": {
      "url": "./node_modules/.store/@types-react@18.3.3/package"
    }
  }
}
```

#### How resolution would work

When a package map is configured and TypeScript runs into a bare specifier (anything that isn't relative, absolute, or a Node built-in) in some file:

1. **Find the importing package.** This is the map entry whose `url` contains the importing file (the longest match wins). If the file isn't inside any mapped package, the import doesn't resolve. Node throws `ERR_PACKAGE_MAP_EXTERNAL_FILE` in this case, and TypeScript would report a diagnostic.
2. **Look up the specifier's package name** (`foo` in `foo/bar`, `@scope/foo` in `@scope/foo/bar`) in that entry's `dependencies`. If it isn't there, the import doesn't resolve. TypeScript reports the usual "Cannot find module" error, ideally with an extra note that the package isn't declared as a dependency of the importing package.
3. **Get the package root** from the target entry's `url`.
4. **Resolve the subpath** from that root with the existing logic for the active `moduleResolution`: `exports`, conditions, `types`, `typesVersions`, and so on.

`@types` fallback works the same way. If `foo` doesn't provide its own types, TypeScript would look up `@types/foo` in the **importing package's** `dependencies`, instead of searching every `node_modules/@types` folder up the tree. Automatic inclusion of global `@types` packages (the default when `types` isn't set) would read the root package's `@types/*` dependencies from the map instead of listing `typeRoots` directories.

Relative imports, absolute paths, `paths` mappings, and `node:` built-ins wouldn't change, the same way Node leaves them alone.

#### Why a static file matters

Because the map is a plain data file with no code to run, TypeScript can implement it natively in both the JS and Go codebases, without plugins, without calling out to a package manager, and without running user code. Watch mode and tsserver only need to watch one file instead of a tree of `node_modules` directories: when the file changes, resolutions get invalidated. And resolution becomes a couple of hash lookups instead of a series of `stat` calls up the directory tree, many of which fail.

#### Multiple package IDs for the same URL

The format lets several package IDs share the same `url`. Package managers use this when the same files on disk need to see different dependencies, for example when a package's peer dependencies are satisfied differently depending on who imports it. Node handles this by keying module instances by *(url, package ID)* and passing the package ID along from each resolution to the next.

For TypeScript, that would mean the same file path could need to be checked in more than one dependency context. That's a much bigger change to how source files are identified, so I'd suggest doing it in two phases:

- **Phase 1:** support maps where each `url` belongs to exactly one package ID. This is the common case, and it already covers isolated, pnpm-style layouts. When a file falls under several entries, TypeScript could report a diagnostic, or merge the entries' `dependencies` as a best-effort fallback.
- **Phase 2:** full support, possibly built on the existing machinery for redirected/duplicated packages, but applied the other way around (one path, several identities).

### 📃 Motivating Example

> **TypeScript now understands package maps**
>
> Package managers like Yarn and pnpm can now generate a *package map*: a single JSON file that describes exactly which packages every package can import, and where they live on disk. Node.js reads it with `--experimental-package-map`, and now TypeScript can too:
>
> ```jsonc
> {
>   "compilerOptions": {
>     "packageMap": "./node_modules/.package-map.json"
>   }
> }
> ```
>
> With this option, TypeScript resolves your imports exactly the way Node will at runtime. Did you forget to add `lodash` to your `package.json`, and it only worked because some other package happened to hoist it? TypeScript now flags that import as an error, before it breaks in production:
>
> ```ts
> import debounce from "lodash/debounce";
> //                   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
> // error: Cannot find module 'lodash/debounce'.
> //   'lodash' is not a dependency of 'my-app' in the package map.
> ```
>
> Auto-imports only suggest packages you've actually declared, and declaration emit no longer writes `import("...")` references to packages your consumers might not be able to resolve. Since TypeScript doesn't need to crawl `node_modules` anymore, module resolution in large monorepos is also faster.

### 💻 Use Cases

1. **What do you want to use this for?**

   - **Matching the runtime.** When a project runs with `--experimental-package-map`, Node won't resolve undeclared ("phantom") dependencies, and it may resolve a specifier to a different version than whatever `node_modules` lookup would find first. If TypeScript keeps walking `node_modules`, it can accept imports that fail at runtime, or check code against the wrong version of a package's types.
   - **Strict dependency checks in monorepos.** Every workspace gets exactly the dependencies it declares. With hoisting, TypeScript can't tell this today.
   - **Package-manager-agnostic support for non-`node_modules` layouts.** Layouts like Yarn PnP or content-addressable stores currently need either TypeScript patches or a compatibility `node_modules` tree (see #28289, open since 2018). Package maps give TypeScript a standard, declarative format that doesn't depend on any particular package manager, so it doesn't have to know about any of them.
   - **Correct module specifiers in auto-imports and declaration emit.** Generating a specifier becomes a reverse lookup: "which key in the importer's `dependencies` points at the package that contains this file?" If there's no such key, the package isn't reachable from the importer. That makes it easy to rule out bad auto-import suggestions, and to report "the inferred type of X cannot be named without a reference to Y" errors accurately.
   - **Performance.** Resolving through a map skips the many `stat`/`realpath` calls (most of them failing) that `node_modules` resolution needs. That's especially true with symlinked layouts, where TypeScript also has to resolve real paths to dedupe packages.

2. **What shortcomings exist with current approaches?**

   - `paths` can't express a per-package dependency graph. It applies to the whole project, maps specifiers to files rather than to package roots (so `exports`/conditions get bypassed), and can't model two packages depending on two different versions of the same dependency.
   - `node_modules` resolution allows whatever the hoisting happens to make reachable, so it can't detect undeclared dependencies. With symlinked layouts, it also depends on `preserveSymlinks` and real-path resolution, which are a common source of duplicate-type and "cannot be named" errors.
   - Yarn PnP support needs a patched TypeScript or editor SDKs, because the PnP data is meant to be consumed through a runtime JS API, not as a static file. Package maps fix this by being a static file that Node itself specifies.

3. **What workarounds are you using in the meantime?**

   - [Forking TypeScript](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/pull/63919) 🥲
   - Making the package manager write out a full `node_modules` tree just so TypeScript (and other tools) can resolve imports, even when the runtime itself uses the package map.
   - Using lint rules (like `import/no-extraneous-dependencies`) or package-manager-level checks to catch undeclared dependencies that the type checker misses.

The plugin manager introduced by #41 is confusing and overcomplicated. Entry lists, runtime states, dependency graphs, configuration editing, lifecycle actions, recovery, and catalog controls compete for attention.

Redesign the manager aggressively enough to bring the most salient information forward. Introduce advanced information and controls when they are relevant, rather than presenting the full diagnostic interface at once.

Develop the redesign collaboratively with a model that has strong UI-design judgment. Establish a coherent default design language based on established interface-design principles, with consistent layout, spacing, typography, color, and control states. labels.description: One agreed capability or internal contract

labels.name: size:M

items.body:
## Metadata

- State: blocked
- Tracker role: curated implementation child of RFC-0019
- Kind: implementation
- Area: Packages / Interop
- Priority: P2
- Size: M
- Parent: none
- Decision: RFC-0019, `rfcs/0019-dependency-foreign-grants.md`, recorded by PR #1722 for #1712
- Blocked by: #1723, #1724, #1457
- Related: RFC-0012 and its amendment A01 (KIF tag `0x800A`); #1422 (`E2S174`); `spec/native-toolchain-v1/contract.json` (*"source-free dependency build from KIF and package artifacts"*)
- Audited against: `origin/main@7d2caf6f3fa3bf733533b08ccf20b6551c3e13f0` (2026-10-04)

## Goal

The package resolver computes every package's **effective grant** over the resolved dependency graph, as RFC-0019 §3 defines it. It then refuses two things, before anything is compiled:

- an edge that grants `foreign` from a package whose effective grant is `plain`;
- a package whose effective grant is `plain` and which contributes any module whose KIF tag `0x800A` is `raw-foreign`.

The second check reads only KIF bytes, never dependency source (answer 6).

## Why it cannot start yet

Three things are missing, and only two of them have issues:

1. **The grant field: #1723.** There is no grant to propagate until a manifest can write one.
2. **The diagnostics band: #1724.** This issue registers its two refusals in that band.
3. **A resolver that can hold a source-package graph: #1457, and more.** `package/manager.sh` resolves *"direct and one level"*, and its only kind is `static-library`. #1457 moves it into Kofun. A dependency that has modules and KIF, and a transitive graph to propagate over, is source-package resolution. No issue owns that at the audited commit: the only open `area:packages` issues at 2026-10-04T07:15Z were #1457 and #1712.

When #1723, #1724, and #1457 have closed, re-refine this issue. File the source-package resolution issue if it still does not exist, name it on the blocker line, and re-measure the evidence below.

## Current behavior and evidence

Measured on `origin/main@7d2caf6f3fa3bf733533b08ccf20b6551c3e13f0`, 2026-10-04:

```sh
task kif-module-trust-profile
# PASS: native toolchain decision contract (kif-module-trust)
# PASS: kif-module-trust ran 8 of 21 mutations (1 its own, 7 shared) and each failed closed

task raw-imports
# PASS: a raw-foreign module is reachable only through `trusted import`, the marker is refused on an
#   ordinary module, the decision is taken from the serialized trust class and the resolved ModuleId,
#   and no refusal publishes an artifact, and `extern "C" fn` requires the class it asks importers to accept

git grep -n -i -E 'trust|security|grant' -- package/manager.sh
# no matches, exit 1
```

What this shows:

- **The fact exists.** Every module's KIF already carries `ordinary` or `raw-foreign` in its required tag `0x800A`, and admission is decided from the serialized class.
- **The fact is enough.** `E2S174` (`bootstrap/stage2/imports_qualified.c`, #1422) refuses an `extern "C" fn` in a module without `trust raw-foreign`. So `0x800A = ordinary` means the module has no `extern "C"`, and the check needs no other per-module fact.
- **The resolver does not read it.** It reads no trust fact at all.

`package/README.md` § *Current boundary* says: *"Resolution is direct and one level: no registry, version ranges, transitive dependencies, install scripts, extraction, or package-provided build steps."*

## Scope

- **Effective grants**, computed exactly as RFC-0019 §3 states:
  - every package starts at `foreign`;
  - each round lowers a package to the meet of its incoming edge grants and its consumers' current levels, with an absent grant counting as `plain`;
  - the root is never lowered.

  The result is independent of the order in which manifests declare dependencies.
- **The escalation refusal.** It names:
  - the package;
  - the edge that grants `foreign`;
  - the path from the root that made the package `plain`.
- **The `0x800A` check.** Read the tag from every module that each `plain` package contributes, through the KIF reader the resolver uses. A `raw-foreign` value is refused. The message names:
  - the package;
  - the module's `ModuleId` and display path;
  - the path from the root.

  A missing or unknown value is RFC-0012/A01's rebuild-required rejection, unchanged.
- **Registration.** Register both refusals in the #1724 band, each with a fixture and a golden.
- **No partial output.** A refusal happens before any compilation of the consumer, and writes no lock file and no build output.

Out of scope:

- **Parsing the grant field** (#1723).
- **The band itself** (#1724).
- **Source-package resolution itself.** That means versions, mounts, fetching source packages, and producing their KIF.
- **The native Core `__linux_syscall*` intrinsics, the macro sandbox, and prebuilt-KIF provenance.** RFC-0019 lists all three as unresolved questions.
- **Any change to KIF, RFC-0012, or the compiler.**

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Façade fixture.** A dependency `D` is reached without a grant, so it is `plain`. Its only foreign code is a `trust raw-foreign` module behind an ordinary façade. `D` is refused, with its source absent and only its KIF and package artifacts present. The message names `D`, the raw module's `ModuleId` and display path, and the path from the root. A version of this gate without this fixture proves nothing RFC-0019 adds.
- [ ] Granting `D` `foreign` makes the same graph resolve and build.
- [ ] **Escalation fixture**, mirroring Flix's `museum` → `museum-restaurant`:
  - The root reaches `P` without a grant. `P`'s manifest grants `Q` `foreign`. This is refused, naming `P`, the edge `P → Q`, and the edge `root → P`.
  - Granting `P` `foreign` makes it resolve.
- [ ] **Meet fixture.**
  - A shared package `S` that contains a `raw-foreign` module, reached along one `foreign` path and one `plain` path, is refused.
  - Removing the `plain` path makes it resolve.
- [ ] A dependency module KIF with `0x800A` missing is rejected as rebuild-required (RFC-0012/A01). It is never treated as `ordinary`.
- [ ] Permuting every manifest's dependency order leaves each outcome and message byte-identical.
- [ ] **Mutation.** Replacing the `0x800A` read with a constant `ordinary` makes the gate fail. This is proved by running it, as `task raw-imports` already does for import admission.
- [ ] Both refusals are registered in the #1724 band with fixtures and goldens, and `task diagnostics` passes.
- [ ] No refusal writes a lock file or build output.

## Validation

| Check | Command | Expected result |
|---|---|---|
| grant propagation and KIF check | a new task this issue adds (proposed name `package-grants`) | PASS: every fixture above, and the mutation fails closed |
| registered refusals | `task diagnostics` | PASS |
| trust facts unchanged | `task kif-module-trust-profile`, `task raw-imports`, `task raw-re-exports` | PASS |
| manifest field unchanged | `task packages` | PASS |
| structural obligations | `task preflight` | PASS. A new task needs a help-group entry and a regenerated release evidence pack (`task release-evidence`) |
| repository | `task verify` | pass |

## Dependencies

- Blocked by: #1723, #1724, #1457
- Not yet filed: source-package resolution, meaning a dependency kind with modules and KIF, and a transitive graph. See *Why it cannot start yet*.
- Decision: RFC-0019 (PR #1722, #1712).

items.title: [UX] resolve --dry-run output full dependency graph as a plan, consumable by unpack
items.body:
## Summary 🤖 

 grcli should behave like a typical package manager for Gemara artifact dependencies: resolve → lock → sync. Given a root artifact, compute its full transitive dependency graph, record what was found as a durable lockfile, then make a local directory match that lockfile exactly -- fetch what's missing, verify it, and remove what's no longer needed. Fetching/verifying/writing should be one reusable operation driven entirely by a lockfile -- not something resolve and unpack each implement separately.

The lockfile should also work disconnected from the network: a fully offline directory (or archive) plus its lockfile should be independently re-verifiable by anyone, with no need to trust whoever produced it.

## Why

A caller should be able to see the full resolved dependency set — every version, every conflict, every license — before any content is fetched. That preview becomes the input to the fetch/sync step, so the expensive graph-walk only ever has to happen once per resolution. It also gives a natural hook for auditing (license compatibility across the whole graph) before committing to anything, and gives downstream tooling (policy engines, offline/airgapped consumers) a stable, inspectable artifact to build on instead of having to re-derive it.

This covers some of the authoring flows for compliance-as-code: reading a single artifact, and syncing a project's full dependency set to disk. grcli's responsibility ends at producing a correct, verified, synced tree plus its lockfile. Aggregation or derived artifacts can be part of consumer workflow.

## Open Questions

  - Can the full resolved graph (versions, digests, licenses) be known without fetching full artifact content, or does that require a cheaper metadata-only lookup per dependency?
  - When the resolved graph disagrees with itself (same dependency pinned to two different versions), should the fetch/sync step refuse to proceed, or proceed and surface the disagreement for something downstream to handle?
  - When syncing a local directory to match a lockfile, should content no longer referenced by the lockfile be removed automatically, and if so, how does a caller preview that removal before it happens?
  - Should re-verifying an already-fetched, offline dependency set require any network access at all, or must it be fully self-contained?

Migrate the Capacitor iOS project from CocoaPods to Swift Package Manager (SPM). Capacitor 8 supports SPM and uses it by default for new iOS projects.

This is not an immediate build-breaking change: existing CocoaPods packages and builds will remain available. CocoaPods trunk is scheduled to become read-only on December 2, 2026, so new pod versions will no longer be published there. Firebase plans to stop publishing CocoaPods releases in October 2026.

Most installed Capacitor plugins already ship a `Package.swift`. Two dependencies currently block a clean migration:

Preference: wait for Capawesome barcode scanner SPM support rather than replace it now. A Zeroconf fork is acceptable when migration work begins.

### Package ecosystem

npm_and_yarn (yarn classic, lockfile v1)

### Package manager version

yarn 1.22 lockfile, generated by the Kotlin Gradle plugin 2.x (`kotlinUpgradeYarnLock`)

### Language version

Kotlin Multiplatform, `js()` target

### Manifest location and content before the Dependabot update

`kotlin/kotlin-js-store/yarn.lock` in https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation (public). Kotlin Multiplatform keeps the lockfile of its JavaScript test toolchain (Mocha, Karma, webpack) in `kotlin-js-store/yarn.lock` and commits it, as JetBrains documents: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/js-project-setup.html#version-locking-via-kotlin-js-store. The matching `package.json` is generated at build time under `build/js/` and is not committed. The directory holds only the lockfile.

### dependabot.yml content

The directory is not configured in `dependabot.yml`. The jobs below are the security updates GitHub starts for the alerts the dependency graph raises on that lockfile.

### Updated dependency

minimatch (GHSA-g3hv-75wg-m249), glob (GHSA-3g3m-2fjr-6pw4), diff (GHSA-73rr-hh4g-fpgx)

### What you expected to see, versus what you actually saw

The dependency graph reads the lockfile and raises Dependabot alerts on it. Every security update job for those alerts then fails:

```
Job definition: {"job":{"command":"security", ... "dependencies":["minimatch"], ... "source":{ ... "directories":["/kotlin/kotlin-js-store"]}}}
ERROR <job_1674697167> Error during file fetching; aborting: /kotlin/kotlin-js-store/package.json not found
| dependency_file_not_found | { "message": "/kotlin/kotlin-js-store/package.json not found" } |
```

Runs:

- https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/actions/runs/41478063329 (minimatch)
- https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/actions/runs/41478058464 (glob)
- https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/actions/runs/41478058822 (diff)

The failure repeats on every run, and the alerts stay open with no explanation in the alert itself.

What I expected, either:

1. the lockfile alone gets updated: for yarn classic, re-resolve the vulnerable entries in `yarn.lock` within the ranges already recorded there; or
2. the job ends with a specific, documented error (for example `dependency_file_not_supported` with the message "yarn.lock has no package.json beside it; it is generated by another build tool, so raise the version there") instead of a generic "file not found", and the alert says why no pull request can be opened.

### Native package manager behavior

`yarn install` needs a `package.json`. The Kotlin Gradle plugin regenerates the lockfile from `build/js/package.json`, with `resolutions` taken from `YarnRootExtension.resolution(...)`.

### Smallest manifest that reproduces the issue

A repository containing only `sub/yarn.lock`, with one locked package affected by an advisory:

```
# yarn lockfile v1


minimatch@^9.0.4:
  version "9.0.5"
  resolved "https://registry.yarnpkg.com/minimatch/-/minimatch-9.0.5.tgz"
```

Once the dependency graph raises the alert, the security update fails with `/sub/package.json not found`.

### Workaround

Raise the versions in the tool that generates the lock. In Kotlin, add `resolution("minimatch", "^11.0.4")` to `YarnRootExtension`, then run `./gradlew rootPackageJson --rerun kotlinUpgradeYarnLock`. Audit the lockfile in CI with the registry's bulk advisory endpoint, as `npm audit` cannot read it either. links-notation does both in https://github.com/link-foundation/links-notation/pull/378 (`scripts/ci/audit-yarn-lock.mjs`).

### Suggested fix

In `NpmAndYarn::FileFetcher`, when the directory has a `yarn.lock` and no `package.json`, raise `Dependabot::DependencyFileNotSupported` with the message above instead of `DependencyFileNotFound`. The security update service can then report it on the alert, and stop treating the job as failed. A fuller fix would be a lockfile-only update path for yarn classic: rewrite the vulnerable entries within their recorded ranges, as `yarn upgrade <name>` does for a transitive dependency.

items.title: Analyzer: Add a cyclonedx-py based Python package manager

type.name: Enhancement
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
ORT's Python analysis currently relies on Python Inspector (see #11467), and it does not cover newer package managers like `uv` and `pdm` (#11027). The idea is to add a Python package manager that uses [cyclonedx-py](https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-python) to produce the dependency data as an alternative.

cyclonedx-py generates a CycloneDX SBOM from a Python project, either statically from a `poetry.lock` / `Pipfile.lock` / `requirements.txt`, or from an installed virtual environment (complete, and with license data). ORT already has the machinery to turn a CycloneDX SBOM into its own model: `CycloneDxPackageManager` in `utils/cyclonedx`, currently used by the `Mix` and `Rebar3` managers. A cyclonedx-py based manager would work the same way: run the tool, get a CycloneDX SBOM, hand it to that engine. The most useful mode is `environment`: install the project (with pip / poetry / uv / ...) and scan the venv, which gives the full transitive closure regardless of the package manager.

The main benefit is `uv` / `pdm` coverage. ORT classifies such projects as `Unmanaged`, while cyclonedx-py produces a complete SBOM with licenses and the dependency graph. This complements #11027 rather than replacing the case for native uv support. It is a working path in the meantime.

This held up in testing: cyclonedx-py matched or exceeded ORT's Python Inspector result wherever ORT could analyze the project, and covered projects ORT could not analyze at all.

A working prototype of the import side already exists: a small package manager (~35 lines) on top of the existing `CycloneDxPackageManager`, plus a fix for SBOMs with no root component (which cyclonedx-py's `environment` mode emits). It compiles into ORT and reproduces the expected package set and dependency graph. 

Whoever implements this will need the project's own package manager (uv, poetry, pip) to run before the new manager, so the environment is populated before it gets scanned. For example, a uv project needs uv to run first.

The main tradeoff is that the complete `environment` mode installs the project first, so it runs the project's build, the same as `Mix` and `Rebar3` already do. A few things to keep in mind:

- Platform/architecture specific packages (Windows/macOS only, arm/x86 only) are only captured for the platform the analysis runs on.
- Heavy packages (e.g. TensorFlow) make the install slow and resource intensive.
- The Python version used for the install matters, since a `requirements.txt` can pin different packages per version.
- It does not help for projects that cannot be installed and have no lockfile, so Python Inspector stays useful as a fallback there.

Alternatives considered: keep Python Inspector, add a separate native manager per tool (#11027, one resolver each), or generate the CycloneDX outside ORT and import it with a generic CycloneDX file manager (works, but leaves generation as a manual pre-step).

items.title: Implement an optional package repository and lightweight dependency planner library
items.body:
## Implementation audit — 2026-10-28 (repository client still missing)

**Current baseline:** [`xila-project/packages`](https://github.com/xila-project/packages) has an **unsigned, direct-addressable static preview**, generated by Python from TOML declarations ([packages#1](https://github.com/xila-project/packages/pull/1)). It is **not** an authenticated repository; no package descriptors are currently committed under `packages/` beyond `.gitkeep`. [package_manager#25](https://github.com/xila-project/package_manager/pull/25) added host-side bundle creation, not an index client or resolver. The shared `crates/manager` currently explicitly states **no public installer API**. No authenticated index reader, repository configuration, dependency planner or repository-mediated install can be credited as implemented.

**Next executable steps:**
- [ ] Align a signed **per-package direct-addressable metadata schema**, key delegations and anti-rollback policy with [#19](https://github.com/xila-project/package_manager/issues/19) and registry publication [packages#3](https://github.com/xila-project/packages/issues/3); keep format/manifest authority in [#27](https://github.com/xila-project/package_manager/issues/27).
- [ ] Implement a portable bounded `no_std` authenticated descriptor reader and a **local/offline first** deterministic package/version selector. Do not assume the registry preview authorizes installs.
- [ ] Gate remote transport, caching and dependency planning independently; avoid mandatory HTTP/TLS and large in-memory catalogs.
- [ ] Only add end-to-end download/install/upgrade after [core#491](https://github.com/xila-project/core/issues/491) supplies a tested offline transactional installer. Negative tests must cover forged metadata, replaced archives, duplicate namespaces, staleness and unsatisfiable plans.

**Keep open.** This issue owns reusable repository *client* behavior, not registry publication CI or VFS transactions.

---
## Goal

Design an **optional `libraries/package_repository`** layer for repository configuration, authenticated index retrieval, application discovery, version selection and lightweight dependency planning. It is the **APT-like orchestration layer**, not the local installer or a second archive parser.

This should be deferred until offline package installation works (#308 and the local installer issue). The format and trust protocol must remain compatible with xila-project/package_manager#27 and xila-project/package_manager#28.

## Responsibilities

- Configure/list/remove repositories and their trust anchors; do not trust keys carried by untrusted index downloads.
- Fetch or consume repository indexes with **authenticated metadata** and recorded source identity; HTTPS alone is insufficient to replace package signature policy.
- Search, inspect versions, select update candidates and produce a bounded **installation plan**.
- Download/stream selected artifacts through a transport interface into the local installer without forcing a complete package/cache into RAM.
- Resolve simple mandatory dependencies and exact/minimum/version-range constraints only when justified; detect cycles, conflicts, duplicate providers and unsatisfiable plans.
- Support offline indexes/mirrors and local repositories. Optional caching must have explicit byte/entry limits.
- Provide rollback/freeze resistance proportional to target capabilities (authenticated index versions, monotonic counters or trusted clock). Document limitations if secure time or tamper-resistant persistence is unavailable.
- Keep firmware code size, RAM/stack and network connections small and bounded.

## Architectural boundaries

- **Depends on:** the local installer's API for actual changes; xila-project/package_manager#27 for format/index contract; xila-project/package_manager#28 for verification primitives.
- **Does not own:** local installation transactions or installed-file DB, executable launch checks, low-level archive decoding, cryptographic algorithm implementation, the CLI, or a background daemon.
- Transport is injected/adapted (network or local file); no hard dependency on HTTP/TLS in the pure planner core.
- Feature-gate network, index parsing and dependency planner separately when useful; minimal configurations omit this library entirely.
- Avoid porting libapt, APT's full resolver or a SAT solver for MVP. An explicitly bounded simpler planner is preferable; refuse unmanageable graphs predictably.

## Scope and security decisions

- Agree one versioned signed repository-index format and stable package IDs, version ordering, target/ABI filters, digests and repository-key scoping with xila-project/package_manager#27.
- Decide precedence and collision policy across third-party repositories. Repository trust **does not grant runtime filesystem/device permissions**.
- Offline installs bypass this library and should behave identically whether a package arrived over HTTP or from disk.
- Document whether the planner can use an on-disk index, repeated sequential scans, or a limited-size in-memory graph; benchmark the options.
- Authenticate plans against index snapshots and verify downloaded artifact identity/hash before and during installation to prevent substitution.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Authenticated repository index with streaming/bounded reads, offline use and clear trust model.
- [ ] Search/list/inspect available packages and versions without a full index resident in RAM.
- [ ] Deterministic simple dependency planner with cycle/conflict/missing-package detection and strict memory/work limits.
- [ ] End-to-end repository install/upgrade delegates all local mutations to the installer.
- [ ] No daemon and no mandatory dependency on network/TLS or a heavyweight solver in offline builds.
- [ ] Tests for altered indexes, package substitution, stale/downgraded metadata, malformed dependency graphs and interrupted downloads.
- [ ] Native and embedded footprint/latency measurement or documented hardware limitations.

## Related
- xila-project/core#308 — overall package manager tracking.
- xila-project/package_manager#27 — signed package metadata and format.
- xila-project/package_manager#28 — signature/hash verifier.
- xila-project/core#307 — streaming HTTP clients, if transport work is reused.

labels.name: in-house
labels.description: Maintainer-handled internal work - not open for contribution

items.body:
> Note: this is an in-house item already being handled by the maintainer - not open for contribution. Filed for tracking only.

CycloneDX output carries no dependency relationships at all. `src/output/cyclonedx.ts` never calls `resolveDependencyEdges` and never emits a `dependencies` array.

## Measured

`examples/analog`, 3368 packages, a project with a properly named `package.json`:

```
CycloneDX metadata.component: analogjs-platform
CycloneDX dependencies entries: 0
```

Same project, SPDX: every package has a parent edge except the root.

Verified structurally as well:

```
$ grep -c 'resolveDependencyEdges' src/output/cyclonedx.ts src/output/spdx.ts
src/output/cyclonedx.ts:0
src/output/spdx.ts:1
```

## Why it matters

CycloneDX 1.6 defines a `dependencies` array precisely for this, and it is what Dependency-Track builds its graph from. `website/docs/cyclonedx.md` points users at Dependency-Track as the headline integration, so the format is being recommended for the tool that most depends on the field we do not emit.

Dependency relationships are also an NTIA minimum element. The SPDX output was brought to completeness across all four package managers in #1106, #1115, #1125 and #1132. CycloneDX was never part of that, and nothing said so.

## Scope note, in fairness

`cyclonedx.md` does not claim to emit a dependency graph, so no documentation is wrong. But the SBOM work has been described in several PR bodies and tracker entries as completing "dependency graphs" without qualifying the format, which reads broader than it is. Worth correcting in the v1.35.0 release notes so nobody infers CycloneDX parity.

## Fix direction

The hard part is already done. `resolveDependencyEdges` returns `{ child, parent }` keyed by `name@version` and is format-agnostic. CycloneDX needs the same call, then a mapping from those pairs to `dependencies[].ref` and `dependsOn`, using the same purl `bom-ref` values the components already carry. The root component becomes the anchor for `parent: null`, mirroring SPDX.

Note #1134 applies here too: a project with no `package.json` name has no root component to anchor to.

items.title: idea: package-manager-neutral workspace discovery with Nx as task/graph layer
items.body:
## Idea

Separate package/workspace discovery from task and project-graph execution instead of teaching `@snailicid3/workspace` package-manager-specific CLI output formats.

### Proposed split

```text
package/workspace inventory
  -> @manypkg/get-packages
  -> snailicid3 Zod manifest/workspace schemas
  -> WorkspaceSnapshot

project/task graph + execution
  -> Nx / Nx Devkit
  -> affected, dependency graph, task orchestration, caching

package-manager-native operations
  -> pnpm / npm / Yarn / Bun
  -> install, add/remove dependencies, lockfile, pack/publish where appropriate
```

### Why consider `@manypkg/get-packages`

Changesets already uses the Manypkg ecosystem for package-manager-neutral monorepo discovery. It can normalize package enumeration across pnpm, npm, Yarn, Bun and other workspace layouts, avoiding `pnpm list --json`-style parsing in snailicid3.

`@manypkg/get-packages` should remain an implementation detail: snailicid3's own Zod schemas/types stay the public/canonical model.

### Nx boundary

Do not make an Nx project graph synonymous with a package-manager workspace. An Nx project is not necessarily a publishable JS package.

Use Nx where its model is actually useful:

- task execution (`build`, `test`, `lint`, etc.)
- caching and task dependencies
- project dependency graph
- affected/change analysis when Nx semantics are desired
- CI orchestration

Keep package manifests/workspace package discovery as a separate repository fact.

### Single-package repos

Nx is still potentially useful in single-package repositories. The main benefits are task caching, task dependencies/orchestration, inferred tasks/plugins, consistent commands across repos, and CI caching. `nx affected` has much less pruning value when there is only one project because most relevant source changes affect that project.

This could make Nx a consistent task layer across both single-package repos and monorepos without requiring every repo to become a workspace/monorepo.

### Questions before implementation

- Compare `@manypkg/get-packages` output/behavior with current `getWorkspacePackagesList()` requirements.
- Decide whether package-manager detection comes from Manypkg or Nx utilities.
- Identify which current `runPackageManager()` callers are true package-manager operations versus task execution/discovery that should move elsewhere.
- Decide where Nx Devkit APIs are preferable to spawning `nx` CLI commands from library code.
- Keep this independent from the immediate scope-classifier cleanup (#212) unless implementation naturally overlaps.

items.body:
> **Category:** Interoperability · **Type:** bug · **Priority:** P1 · **Effort:** M
> **Audit id:** ISSUE-070 · proposed in the repository audit at `8fb6167`

**Summary**

sdk/interop imports @nestjs, cache-manager and @stellar/stellar-sdk, none of which are dependencies, and the folder is outside the TypeScript build.

**Problem statement**

The four files in `sdk/interop/` implement a Universal Resolver driver and a DID service using `@nestjs/common`, `@nestjs/cache-manager`, `cache-manager` and `@stellar/stellar-sdk`. None of those packages appear in `package.json` (dependencies or devDependencies), and the root `tsconfig.json` includes only `sdk/src/**/*`, so the folder is never type-checked or built. The module also differs from the rest of the SDK in its base library (`@stellar/stellar-sdk` versus the widely used `stellar-sdk`), so even if it were compiled it would pull a second copy of the SDK into the dependency graph. This is a large, uncompiled interop surface that looks maintained.

**Evidence**

- sdk/interop/did-stellar.service.ts:1-6 — imports `@nestjs/common`, `@nestjs/cache-manager`, `cache-manager`, `@stellar/stellar-sdk`
- package.json — none of those packages are declared
- tsconfig.json — `include: ["sdk/src/**/*"]` excludes sdk/interop
- sdk/interop/did-stellar.controller.ts / .module.ts / universal-resolver.interface.ts — present but never built

**Proposed solution**

Either promote the interop module into the product (declare the dependencies, add it to the build and test config, align on a single Stellar SDK package, and cover it with tests) or move it out of the published SDK into an example or a separate package with its own manifests. If Universal Resolver interop is in scope, add a contract test against the resolver interface.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ] Every import in the interop module resolves against a declared dependency.
- [ ] The module is either type-checked and tested in CI, or removed from the SDK tree.
- [ ] Only one Stellar SDK package is used across the repository.
- [ ] The Universal Resolver interface is either implemented, tested and documented, or explicitly marked unsupported.

**Testing requirements**

Add the folder to a tsconfig project and run `tsc --noEmit` in CI; if adopted, add unit tests for DID resolution and caching.

**Dependencies**

Aligns with the dependency-consistency work.

**Related existing issues:** #105, #102, #98

## Why

Bowire has the keyring — `{{keyring.*}}` resolves a secret from the machine's credential store, and `bowire test --keyring` reads them in CI. That solves the single-developer case well.

It does not solve the team case. Bruno integrates HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault and AWS Secrets Manager; Yaak integrates 1Password. A team does not put its staging credentials in every developer's local keychain — it puts them in one place and grants access.

Half the story is there. The missing half is the one an organisation asks about.

## What

- [ ] A **variable source seam** for external secret stores, mirroring the existing `{{keyring.*}}` / `{{ai.*}}` sources: `{{vault.path/to/secret#field}}`, `{{akv.<vault>/<name>}}`, `{{awssm.<id>}}`, `{{onepassword.<item>/<field>}}`.
- [ ] **Each provider is its own optional sibling package.** Vault, Azure and AWS SDKs are heavy dependencies; Core must not grow one. Missing package means the source is not offered, with a message saying which package would add it — capabilities stay queryable.
- [ ] Prefer the maintained vendor SDK over hand-rolled HTTP for each provider.
- [ ] Authentication per provider follows that provider's normal chain (Azure `DefaultAzureCredential`, AWS default credential chain, Vault token / AppRole), so CI works without Bowire-specific credential plumbing.
- [ ] Resolution is **read-only, on demand, and cached for the run** — never written back, never bulk-fetched, never persisted to a workspace file.
- [ ] Resolved values are treated exactly as `{{secret.*}}` already is: never resolved into a code export, never written into a recording or report, never echoed by an MCP tool.
- [ ] Works from CLI and MCP as well as the workbench.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A request referencing `{{vault.…}}` resolves against a real Vault dev server in an integration test, and the same reference works under `bowire test`.
- [ ] With the provider package absent, the reference fails with a message naming the package to install — not a null and not a stack trace.
- [ ] No provider SDK appears in Core's dependency graph.
- [ ] A resolved secret never appears in an export, recording, report, or MCP response.

items.title: Research: pixi (or alternatives) as a package-manager backend to reduce RUN shell-outs
items.body:
## Problem

Scripts that need external tools or libraries currently shell out via `RUN` to system package managers (`apt`, `brew`, MSYS2 `pacman`, etc.). That means:

- Global mutable state (`/usr`, registry keys): version conflicts between projects, concurrent builds interfering, sudo requirements.
- Drift: upstream repos move, so the same script resolves different dependencies over time.
- Three package-manager dialects for one cross-platform script.

## Proposal

Research tying OxDock into a portable, per-project package manager — current frontrunner is **[pixi](https://pixi.sh)** (prefix.dev) — so dependency setup becomes declarative and conflict-free instead of imperative shell-outs:

- One Rust binary, no Python involved (neither to run pixi itself nor in the dependency graph unless requested).
- Per-project environments in a folder, lockfile-pinned (`pixi.toml` + `pixi.lock`), identical behavior on Linux/macOS/Windows.
- conda-forge package set covers native toolchains and system libs (compilers, cmake, ninja, glib, pixman, Qt), not just Python.
- `conda-pack` produces relocatable trees with prefix rewriting — close to our portable-output needs.

Alternatives to evaluate alongside: **pkgx** (shim-based, smaller pantry, weaker lockfile story), Nix (rejected for portability: `/nix/store` mount demands, no native Windows), system managers behind prefix installs.

## Division of labor (proposed)

- Package manager owns *environments*: what is installed, pinned, isolated.
- OxDock owns *procedure across machines*: where it runs (REMOTE), what crosses the wire (COPY transfers), what gets asserted.
- Do not duplicate pixi's task runner; keep one orchestrator.

## Research questions

1. Does pixi cover a representative native dependency closure (compilers, cmake, ninja, glib-style system libs) on all of our platform targets?
2. What would the DSL surface look like (`INSTALL` command? `ENV`-style declaration? lockfile-aware caching keyed on script + dependency pins)?
3. How do pixi environments compose with REMOTE guests (per-exec env setup cost, caching across execs)?
4. Does `conda-pack` output actually shortcut portable-tree assembly, or does our last-mile treatment (signing, entitlements, firmware layout) dominate anyway?
5. Pilot candidate: redo one build leg's dependency setup under pixi with build scripts untouched; expand only if the closure reproduces exactly.

## Non-goals

- Mirroring binaries ourselves (trust/provenance burden; prefer recipes over mirrors).
- Replacing OxDock orchestration with pixi tasks.

- Do not repeat Core fuzzing or comprehensive sanitizer suites.
- Keep CLI-specific integration checks.
- Avoid duplicate jobs across PR and release workflows.
- Separate fast PR verification from release-specific checks.
- Reuse trustworthy completed verification results where possible.

### Dependency Graph

- Integrate GitHub Dependency Submission API.
- Report direct dependencies, including:
  - OpenTLV Core.
  - nlohmann_json.
- Include resolved dependency versions or immutable revisions.
- Report applicable transitive dependencies when reliably discoverable.
- Generate dependency metadata from authoritative build/dependency information.
- Do not introduce a manually maintained dependency manifest.
- Avoid submitting misleading or incomplete dependency relationships.
- Use minimum required GitHub Actions permissions.

### CI Efficiency

- Avoid unnecessary dependency downloads.
- Use appropriate caching without compromising correctness.
- Avoid redundant build configurations.
- Ensure failed checks produce actionable diagnostics.
- Keep workflow responsibilities clearly separated.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] CLI workflows do not run comprehensive Core tests.
- [ ] PR CI executes only relevant CLI checks.
- [ ] Release-specific verification is separated appropriately.
- [ ] GitHub Dependency Graph displays OpenTLV Core.
- [ ] GitHub Dependency Graph displays nlohmann_json.
- [ ] Dependency versions or revisions are traceable.
- [ ] Dependency metadata is generated automatically.
- [ ] No duplicate dependency manifest is maintained.
- [ ] CI workflows avoid unnecessary repeated work.
- [ ] Required workflow permissions are documented.

## Out of Scope

- Core CI redesign.
- Core dependency ownership changes.
- Reimplementation of Core tests.
- Package-manager integration.
- Release artifact packaging.

items.title: Pin site package manager and guard frozen lockfile drift
items.body:
## Context

Production issue #236 was repaired by restoring the six pnpm override snapshots in the lockfile. Vercel selected pnpm 10.x by project creation date because `site/package.json` has no exact `packageManager` pin. The site also has both npm and pnpm lockfiles, increasing the chance that a future dependency edit updates the wrong graph.

## Scope

Decide and document one authoritative site package manager and lockfile. Pin the exact supported pnpm version via Corepack in the site manifest and verify Vercel uses it. Reconcile any npm lockfile ownership deliberately, without silently deleting it or downgrading existing security overrides. Add a lightweight frozen-install check that catches a manifest/lockfile override mismatch before production deployment.

## Done when

- Fresh Linux install and Vercel preview use the pinned manager and succeed with a frozen lockfile.
- Security overrides remain resolved; native platform selectors and package integrity are reviewed for unintended churn.
- CI fails on a deliberate override/lockfile mismatch and passes on the corrected graph.
- Repo guidance names the authoritative lockfile and exact update command.

This is a separate maintenance change; do not fold it into the already merged production incident repair.
